value: answer=1. Main complaint: "What's the problem? Where's the pain? When did it start? Does it move? What makes it worse? 0–10?" 2. Red-flag questions (warning signs). S1: fever? yellow skin/eyes? dark urine/pale stools? constant pain over 24 h? pain through to back? S2: pain moved from belly button? vomiting? appetite? fever? urine symptoms? diarrhoea? women: last period, chance of pregnancy, vaginal bleeding, shoulder-tip pain; men: testicle pain. 3. Medicines: everything, especially blood thinners (and when last taken), diabetes medicines, GLP-1 injections, steroids, BP tablets, the pill, herbal remedies. 5. Allergies: what and what happened. 6. Previous anaesthetics: any problems; family members with serious anaesthetic problems. 7. Social: smoking, alcohol, drugs, who's at home. 8. Last food and drink: exact time and what. 9. Pregnancy (whenever pregnancy is possible for this patient): asked privately and sensitively; test offered with consent if there is any doubt CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (NICE NG45). 10. Summarise back and ask "Anything else you want to tell me?"

S1: usually optimise first (defer/re-time); S2: correct in parallel YES NO Anything affecting anaesthesia? value: text=Example Patient A — uncomplicated S1 (everything goes right) Who: Mrs Ayesha Khan, 42, teacher, born 14 March 1984. Why here: three attacks of pain under her right ribs over six months, each after an oily meal, lasting 1–2 hours. Her GP sent her to a surgeon; an ultrasound showed gallstones. She was booked for keyhole gallbladder removal today at 09:00. Scene 1 — Arrival (Step 1) Teacher says: "Okay Ruhan, she has arrived. First, introduce yourself and make sure she's the right person." You ask: "Could you tell me your full name and date of birth?" She says "Ayesha Khan, fourteenth of March 1984." You check the wristband: AYESHA KHAN, 14/03/1984, MR 102938 — matches the notes. You ask about allergies: "None." No allergy band needed. You ask what she's here for: "To have my gallbladder taken out with keyhole." Her husband will take her home and stay overnight. → Identity confirmed. Continue. Scene 2 — Questions (Step 2) What you ask and what she answers - Pain: "Attacks under my right ribs after oily food, settle in an hour or two. None in the last 3 weeks." → typical biliary colic, no current attack. - Red flags: no fever, no yellow eyes, urine normal colour, no back pain. → no sign of complications. - Other illnesses: none. Medicines: none except paracetamol sometimes. Herbal: none. - Previous anaesthetic: caesarean section 2012, no problems. Family: no anaesthetic problems. - Smoking: never. Alcohol: none. - Last food: dinner at 21:00 last night (rice and chicken). Last drink: water at 06:30. Time now: 08:00. → solid food 11 hours ago (≥8 h ✓), clear water 1.5 hours ago… wait — that's less than 2 hours! Teacher says: Good catch moment! Water at 06:30 and surgery at 09:00 means 2.5 hours by the time of anaesthesia — that's fine, because the 2-hour rule applies to the time of anaesthesia, not the time you're asking. Record exact times and let the anaesthetist decide. Pregnancy: you ask privately; last period started 10 days ago, she uses a coil. She agrees to a urine pregnancy test (hospital policy) CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Scene 3 — Vital signs (Step 3) Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 76 /min, regular Normal (51–90) Heart beating calmly Blood pressure 124/78 mmHg Normal Good pressure; not high Breathing rate 14 /min Normal (12–20) Breathing calmly Oxygen saturation 98% on room air Normal (96+) Lungs working well Temperature 36.7 °C Normal No fever → no sign of infection Alertness Alert Normal Brain fine Pain 0/10 Normal No current attack BMI 27 (70 kg, 1.61 m) Overweight (South Asian cut-off 23+) Note for anaesthetist; not a problem NEWS2 0 Low Routine observations Scene 4 — Examination (Step 4) Eyes white (no jaundice). Heart and lungs sound normal. Tummy soft; mild tenderness under right ribs only with deep pressure; Murphy's sign negative. Mouth opens well (3 fingers), Mallampati class 2, neck moves normally. STOP-BANG 1. → Fits uncomplicated gallstones; airway looks easy. Scene 5 — Risk (Step 5) ASA 1 (healthy). Clot risk: low (age under 60, no risk factors other than surgery). Anaesthetist agrees: "ASA 1, standard general anaesthetic." Scene 6 — Tests (Step 6) and results (Step 7) Ordered: liver tests (because she has gallstone disease) and urine pregnancy test (policy). Not ordered: chest X-ray, ECG, clotting, kidney tests — she's healthy and under 65, so these wouldn't change anything CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Test Result Normal What you think Bilirubin 12 µmol/L 3–21 Bile flowing normally ALT 24 U/L ~7–40 Liver cells fine ALP 78 U/L ~30–130 Bile ducts not blocked GGT 22 U/L below 40 (women) Confirms ducts fine Albumin 42 g/L 35–50 Good nutrition Urine pregnancy test Negative — Not pregnant (Ultrasound from clinic) Several stones; wall 2 mm; duct 4 mm wall ≤3 mm; duct ≤6 mm Simple gallstones, duct normal Teacher says: Everything looks acceptable, so we continue. Why? Because: she has the diagnosis we planned for; there's no sign the gallbladder is inflamed (normal temperature, heart rate, no Murphy's sign) or that a stone is in the bile duct (normal liver tests and duct width — 'low risk'); she's healthy (ASA 1); she's fasted; she's not pregnant. Nothing needs fixing or a senior decision. Scene 7 — Treatment/optimisation (Step 8) Nothing to optimise. She needs no regular medicines held. Antibiotic: not needed for a low-risk patient CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Clot prevention: stockings per local policy CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Drip will be placed in the anaesthetic room CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Scene 8 — Consent (Step 9) Pain-free, alert, private room, speaks the language of the consultation fluently (no interpreter needed). You explain diagnosis, the keyhole operation, benefits, main risks with numbers, alternatives (watch and wait), and what happens if nothing is done. She asks: "Can I go home today?" — "Most people can, if you're comfortable and eating." Teach-back: "You'll take out my gallbladder through small cuts; there's a small chance of bile leak or needing a bigger cut." ✓ She signs. Scene 9 — Preparation (Step 10) Gown on; wedding ring taped; no dentures; stockings on; temperature 36.7 ✓; pregnancy test documented; consent present; ID band ✓; documents together. Site marking: not applicable (midline operation) CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Checklist complete. Scene 10 — Theatre ready, transfer, handover (Steps 11–12) Theatre confirms the keyhole tower, CO2 and spare cylinder, suction, warming and anaesthetic machine check. NEWS2 0 → porter + nurse. SBAR to anaesthetist: "S: Ayesha Khan, 42, for laparoscopic cholecystectomy. B: symptomatic gallstones, otherwise well, no allergies, no regular medicines, previous caesarean without problems. A: obs normal, NEWS2 0, last food 21:00, water 06:30, LFTs normal, pregnancy test negative, ASA 1, airway Mallampati 2, consent signed. R: ready for theatre; no antibiotic indicated per protocol; stockings on." Scene 11 — WHO Sign In (Step 13) Question Answer Patient confirms identity, site, procedure, consent? Yes — she says her name, DOB, 'gallbladder keyhole', consent signed Site marked? Not applicable Anaesthesia machine and medication check complete? Yes Oximeter on and working? Yes, 99% Known allergy? No Difficult airway / aspiration risk? No (fasted, Mallampati 2) Risk of >500 mL blood loss? No Scene 12 — WHO Time Out (Step 14) Team introduces itself. Patient, site, procedure confirmed. Surgeon: 'standard lap chole, about 60 minutes, minimal blood loss.' Anaesthetist: 'no concerns.' Nurse: 'sterility indicators confirmed, tower working.' Antibiotic: 'not applicable.' value: text=Example Patient B — abnormal S1 (the 'elective' patient who isn't well today) Who: Mrs Farzana Ahmed, 61, booked for planned keyhole gallbladder removal. Identity confirmed; allergic to nothing. The clue in the history You ask the red-flag questions. "Have your eyes or skin looked yellow?" — "My daughter said my eyes looked a bit yellow last week. And my urine has been dark like tea." "Any fever or shivering?" — "No." "Pain?" — "Some aching under the ribs on and off." Teacher says: We found a possible abnormality. Yellow eyes and dark urine suggest jaundice — bilirubin backing up into the blood. In a gallstone patient, the most likely cause is a stone that has slipped into the main bile duct. This is NOT what she was booked for. Now check this: look at her eyes, measure vitals, and send liver tests. Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 84 Normal Calm Blood pressure 138/84 Normal Fine Breathing 16 Normal Fine Oxygen 97% Normal Fine Temperature 37.2 °C Normal No fever — so probably no infection in the duct (yet) Eyes Yellow tinge to the whites Abnormal Jaundice confirmed on examination Test Result Normal Zone and meaning Bilirubin 72 µmol/L (4.2 mg/dL) 3–21 HIGH (above 68) — bile is backing up ALP 380 U/L ~30–130 About 3× normal — bile duct cells irritated by blockage GGT 410 U/L below 40 Confirms the ALP is coming from the bile system ALT 160 U/L ~7–40 Moderately raised — liver cells irritated by backed-up bile WBC 9.8 4.0–11.0 Normal — no strong sign of infection CRP 12 below 5 Mildly raised INR 1.1 0.8–1.2 Clotting normal (long blockage could raise it) Lipase 45 below ~60 Pancreas not inflamed Ultrasound today Gallstones; common bile duct 9 mm; no stone seen in duct duct ≤6 mm Duct WIDE — something is blocking it lower down Teacher says: This result makes us more concerned. The pattern is 'cholestatic' — the bile-duct numbers (ALP, GGT, bilirubin) are raised more than the liver-cell number (ALT), and the duct is wide. Using the bile-duct-stone risk tool: bilirubin above 68 µmol/L plus a duct wider than 6 mm = HIGH risk of a stone in the duct CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (ASGE 2019). Teacher says: Therefore the next step is: do not proceed with today's planned operation. If the surgeon removed the gallbladder today, the stone in the duct would remain and could cause infection (cholangitis) or pancreatitis. Call the senior surgeon. The usual plan is to clear the duct first with ERCP (a camera through the mouth that pulls the stone out), or to image it with MRCP first if the risk were only intermediate — then remove the gallbladder later (local practice CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION ). Explain this to Mrs Ahmed, document, and safety-net: "If you get a fever, shivering or worse pain, come straight back — that could be an infection in the duct." Mrs Ahmed's decision path Jaundice symptoms in history → examine → yellow eyes Fever, shivers, low BP (cholangitis)? EMERGENCY: sepsis bundle + urgent ERCP YES NO Bilirubin above 68 AND duct above 6 mm? HIGH RISK duct stone → postpone today, senior, ERCP pathway YES NO (not reached for Mrs Ahmed) If missed: If the trainee doesn't ask about yellow eyes and doesn't look, the liver tests (if ordered) would still flag it. If the trainee ignores the abnormal results, the senior/anaesthetist character stops the case and the debrief explains: "A stone left in the duct can cause life-threatening infection."

value: text=Patient S1-E — the planned patient with an inflamed gallbladder What we see: Mrs Rabia, 48. Today: constant pain for 2 days, felt hot overnight. T 38.4, HR 108, BP 118/72, RR 20, SpO2 97%. Murphy's sign positive. WBC 15.2, CRP 96. Ultrasound: wall 6 mm, fluid around gallbladder. How the trainee thinks 1. Fever + fast heart = the body is fighting infection/inflammation. 2. Murphy's positive + right-upper tenderness = local gallbladder inflammation (TG18 group A). 3. Raised WBC and CRP = whole-body inflammation (group B). 4. Ultrasound wall thick + fluid = scan evidence (group C) → definite acute cholecystitis. 5. Grade: WBC 15.2 (not above 18), symptoms under 72 h, no lump, no organ failure → Grade I (mild). 6. Decision: she's not suitable for today's planned list as a routine case — she now has an acute illness. Senior surgeon reviews; antibiotics; she moves to the acute pathway. Early keyhole surgery (often within 72 hours; NICE: within a week) is usually the plan CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . NEWS2 = HR 108 (1) + RR 20 (0) + T 38.4 (1) = 2.

value: text=Example Patient C — emergency S2 (classic appendicitis) Who: Mr Hamza Ali, 19, student. Why here: brought to the Emergency Department by his brother at 10:00 with tummy pain since last night. Scene 1 — Arrival and triage (Step 1) Triage note: '19M, abdominal pain 14 h, HR 108, T 37.9, pain 8/10 — very urgent (see within 10 min)'. He's curled on the trolley holding his lower right tummy. Teacher says: "Okay Ruhan, the patient has arrived and he's in a lot of pain. First, the same identity check as always — but quickly." He says "Hamza Ali, 2nd of June 2007"; wristband matches. Allergies: "None." Then: don't make him wait in pain while you do paperwork. Check he's not allergic, and ask the nurse for pain relief now. Pain relief does not hide the diagnosis CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . Scene 2 — First vital signs (Step 3, done early in emergencies) Measurement Value Zone Plain meaning Heart rate 108, regular Fast (91–110) Body stressed — pain? fever? dehydration? infection? Blood pressure 128/76 Normal Circulation coping Breathing 18 Normal OK Oxygen 98% on air Normal Lungs fine Temperature 37.9 °C Normal-high (fever starts at 38.0) Mild inflammation Alertness Alert Normal — Pain 8/10 Severe Needs pain relief now NEWS2 HR 108 → 1; others 0 → total 1 Low Recheck at least every 4–6 h (we'll do more often because of pain/fluids) Teacher says: The heart rate is high. That doesn't mean a heart problem — possible causes are pain, anxiety, fever, dehydration or infection. Everything else is fine, and he's in severe pain. So the likeliest explanation is pain + inflammation. Treat the pain, give fluids, and re-measure. If the heart rate stays high after that, think harder. Scene 3 — First treatment while we work (Step 8 early) What you do in the first 15–30 minutes 1. Drip (cannula) in; take blood at the same time (FBC, CRP, kidneys/salts, group & save per policy). 2. Pain relief: request analgesia: IV paracetamol is a typical first step (SmPC example in Part 8), plus a stronger painkiller titrated by the clinician PATIENT-SPECIFIC DOSE — CLINICIAN CONTROLLED — the clinician prescribes and the nurse administers. 3. Anti-sickness medicine if nauseated (he vomited once). 4. Start IV fluids (he hasn't eaten or drunk properly since last night). 5. Keep him nil by mouth (he may need surgery). 6. Re-check vital signs after treatment. Scene 4 — The history (Step 2), now he's more comfortable "It started around my belly button around 8 last night, then moved down here [lower right] by the morning. I don't want to eat. I threw up once. Hurts when the car went over bumps." No urine symptoms, no diarrhoea, no testicle pain. No illnesses, no medicines, no previous operations. Last food: chicken and rice at 19:00 last night; last drink: water at 06:00. Teacher says: That's the classic appendicitis story: pain moving from the belly button to the lower right, loss of appetite, vomiting after the pain, pain with movement. But we must still rule out look-alikes. For a young man, check the testicles (twisted testicle can cause tummy pain), urine (stones/infection), and ask about bowel symptoms. Scene 5 — Examination (Step 4) Tender lower right tummy (McBurney's point), mild guarding, rebound medium, Rovsing's sign positive. Rest of tummy soft. Testicles normal. → Localised peritonitis in the lower right — fits appendicitis, not burst. Scene 6 — Tests and results (Steps 6–7) Test Result Normal Meaning WBC 13.6 4.0–11.0 Raised — fighting infection Neutrophils 82% 40–75% First-responder cells high → bacterial CRP (20 h of symptoms) 38 mg/L below 5 Moderate inflammation Haemoglobin 148 g/L 130–170 Normal — no bleeding Creatinine 82 µmol/L 60–110 Kidneys fine Potassium 3.9 3.5–5.3 Normal Urine dipstick Ketones +, otherwise negative Negative Not eating (starvation ketones); no infection/blood Lactate Not needed (no sepsis signs) — — Appendicitis scores (calculated in Part 7.1): AIR 7 (indeterminate), AAS 19 (high). Teacher says: Here's a real-world wrinkle. If the hospital uses AIR, the score says 'unsure — get a scan'. If it uses AAS, it says 'high probability'. The WSES guideline says young patients with high scores may not need a scan in some cases, but many hospitals scan anyway. In our draft (AIR default) the trainee requests an ultrasound CLINICAL INTERPRETATION CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . Ultrasound (60–120 min later): 'Non-compressible appendix 9 mm, surrounding fat inflamed, no free fluid, no abscess.' → Positive — simple (uncomplicated) appendicitis. Scene 7 — Decision (Step 8) Hamza's decision path Story + exam + raised WBC/CRP + positive ultrasound Emergency signs (NEWS2 7+, low BP, sepsis)? Sepsis branch YES NO Complicated on scan (perforation, abscess)? Urgent theatre, longer antibiotics YES NO Simple appendicitis → call senior surgeon (SBAR) → decision: laparoscopic appendectomy Antibiotics now (local choice) → anaesthetist review → consent → theatre promptly (timing per surgeon; WSES 2025: within 24 h of admission when surgery is indicated) Call the senior: "S: Hamza Ali, 19, in ED with probable appendicitis. B: 14 hours of pain moving to the right iliac fossa, anorexia, one vomit, no history. A: HR 108 → 96 after analgesia and fluid, T 37.9, NEWS2 1; localised RIF peritonism; WBC 13.6, CRP 38; AIR 7; ultrasound shows uncomplicated appendicitis. R: I'd like you to review him for laparoscopic appendectomy; I've started antibiotics per protocol and kept him nil by mouth." Scene 8 — Anaesthetic review and fasting Food at 19:00 last night (15 hours ago) and water at 06:00. Even though the time looks enough, he's an emergency patient in pain who has had strong painkillers, so the anaesthetist still treats him as a possible 'full stomach' and plans RSI CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . ASA 1E. Scene 9 — Consent (Step 9) Pain now 3/10, alert → has capacity. Explained: appendicitis; keyhole removal; risks (infection, abscess, bleeding, conversion, bowel injury rare); alternative: antibiotics alone for simple appendicitis — about 7 in 10 avoid surgery at 3 months (CODA: 29% needed surgery by 90 days) but about 4 in 10 have it come back within 5 years (APPAC: 39.1%). Hamza chooses surgery. Teach-back ✓. Signed. Scene 10 — Preparation, handover, Sign In, Time Out Checklist (fast but complete): gown, no jewellery, antibiotic time recorded (e.g. 12:10), fluids running, fasting times recorded. Handover to anaesthetist includes: aspiration risk, antibiotic name and time, fluids given, latest NEWS2. Sign In: aspiration risk YES — RSI equipment and suction ready. Time Out at 12:55: antibiotic given 45 minutes ago (within 60) ✓; ultrasound displayed ✓. → READY FOR INCISION.

value: text=Example Patient D — the deteriorating patient (watch the numbers change) Who: Mr Usman, 34. Three days of tummy pain he 'tried to sleep off'. Arrives at 14:00. Time HR BP RR SpO2 Temp Alert? NEWS2 What's happening 14:00 102 124/78 20 97% 38.3 A 2 Infection, coping. Workup started. 14:45 (no fluids/antibiotics given yet) 116 112/70 22 96% 38.9 A 5 Something has changed. Heart faster, BP lower, breathing faster, fever higher. 15:15 128 92/58 26 94% 39.2 A 10 Sepsis with poor circulation — EMERGENCY 15:45 if nobody acts 138 82/48 30 91% 39.4 Confused 16 Septic shock — near collapse Teacher says: At 14:45, something has changed. No single number screams 'disaster' yet, but look at the trend: heart rate up 14, BP down 12, breathing up, fever up — all pointing the same way. NEWS2 has jumped from 2 to 5, which means 'urgent review'. A patient with three days of pain, fever and a rising heart rate may have a burst appendix. What the trainee should notice and do at 14:45 1. Notice the trend (the game shows the chart; the nurse may say "His NEWS2 is 5 now"). 2. Go and look at him: sweaty? tummy now tender everywhere and rigid? → suggests perforation with spreading peritonitis. 3. Call for help: urgent senior review (NEWS2 5–6). 4. Start the sepsis bundle: blood cultures, lactate, IV antibiotics, fluid bolus (e.g. 500 mL quickly) and re-check, assess breathing and use oxygen per protocol if below the target range, measure urine. 5. Request urgent imaging (CT) if senior wants it — with a nurse escort and monitor because he's unstable. Results: lactate 3.8 (raised — organs short of oxygen); WBC 19.8; CRP 210; creatinine 142 (kidneys struggling). CT: perforated appendix with free fluid. At 15:15 (NEWS2 10 — emergency) 1. Emergency call: senior surgeon + anaesthetist now; critical-care team aware. 2. ABCDE: airway OK; breathing fast — oxygen; circulation — second drip, more fluid boluses with re-checks, antibiotics if not yet given (NICE NG253: within 1 hour for the high-risk tier), catheter for urine output; disability — alert, check sugar; exposure — rigid tummy. 3. This patient needs the source of infection removed urgently (source control = surgery) once resuscitation has started CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED . 4. Consent: if he still has capacity, a brief but complete discussion; if confused, senior follows emergency route CONTEXT-DEPENDENT — INSTITUTIONAL PROTOCOL / CLINICIAN CONFIRMATION . 5. Handover: lactate, fluids given, antibiotic time, NEWS2, kidney injury, aspiration risk. After the correct action BP rises to 108/64 after fluids, HR 112, lactate falls to 2.4 on repeat, urine starts flowing. He goes to theatre urgently. Debrief praises early recognition of the trend. If the trainee fails to act By 15:45 he becomes confused with BP 82/48 (septic shock). Medicines to support BP and intensive care are needed; the debrief shows the timeline: 'sepsis criteria met 14:45; antibiotics given 15:55 (70 minutes late).' If inaction continues, the case ends with a safety debrief.

value: text=Patient S2-B — differential diagnosis / diagnostic diversion: it may NOT be appendicitis (ectopic pregnancy) What we see: Ms Sadia, 24. Lower-right pain, shoulder-tip pain, dizzy. HR 112, BP 98/60. Last period 7 weeks ago. Urine pregnancy test POSITIVE. Hb 104. How the trainee thinks 1. Positive pregnancy test + tummy pain: ectopic pregnancy must be considered and excluded — a differential diagnosis (a mimic of appendicitis, not a complication of it) CLINICAL REFERENCE — SOURCE BACKED (NICE NG126). 2. Shoulder-tip pain = blood in the tummy irritating the diaphragm. 3. Fast heart + lowish BP + low Hb = she may be bleeding inside. 4. STOP the appendicitis pathway. Emergency: call for help, two large drips, crossmatch blood, gynaecology NOW, keep nil by mouth. 5. If the trainee never did the pregnancy test: hard safety failure in the debrief.

value: text=SGLT2 inhibitor taken + poor long-term control (with raised BP) Procedure: Elective laparoscopic cholecystectomy (S1). Clinical plausibility: Type 2 diabetes and hypertension commonly coexist; patients on several diabetes drugs frequently misunderstand fasting instructions, and taking a sulfonylurea while fasting causes hypoglycaemia (JBDS/CPOC). SGLT2 inhibitors are increasingly common and carry euglycaemic-DKA risk when fasting (UK consensus 2025). 1. Case introduction Patient Mr Imran Siddiqui, 58, accountant. Synthetic patient. Why in hospital Planned keyhole gallbladder removal for recurrent biliary colic (ultrasound-confirmed gallstones). Background Type 2 diabetes for 9 years; hypertension for 6 years; BMI 31; ex-smoker. Medicines Metformin, gliclazide (sulfonylurea), dapagliflozin (SGLT2 inhibitor), amlodipine, ramipril. Allergies None known. Pre-assessment instructions Omit gliclazide on the day; omit dapagliflozin the day before and the day of surgery (UK 2025 consensus); fast from food after midnight; water until 06:30. 2. Initial patient presentation 08:05, day-surgery bay. Mr Siddiqui is sitting on the trolley, slightly pale and sweaty, talking normally but says he feels 'a bit shaky and hungry'. He is fully alert and orientated. Breathing looks comfortable. The nurse has done a first set of observations and a finger-prick glucose because he is diabetic. 3. Initial observations [case value — simulator-generated] Measurement Value Reference / scoring band Interpretation and concern level Possible causes What to check next BP 174/102 → repeat 172/100 <140/90 reference; grade 2 160–179/100–109 (ESH 2023) Raised, not severe (<180/110) — moderate concern for planned surgery Chronic hypertension, anxiety, ramipril taken today? GP readings in letter; repeat after rest HR 96 regular 60–100 reference; NEWS2 91–110 = 1 Mildly raised Adrenaline response to low sugar, anxiety Recheck after glucose treated RR 16 12–20 Normal — — Temperature 36.6 °C 36.1–38.0 (NEWS2 0) Normal — no sign of infection — — SpO2 97% air ≥96% (NEWS2 0) Normal — — Capillary glucose 3.6 mmol/L Target 6–10 peri-operatively; <4.0 = hypoglycaemia (JBDS) Hypoglycaemia — immediate concern Gliclazide taken while fasting Ask what he took this morning; recheck after treatment Pain 0/10 0–3 comfortable No attack — — NEWS2 1 (HR) 0 expected in planned patients Low total, but a NEWS2 of 0–1 does not detect hypoglycaemia — glucose is not part of NEWS2 — — Teaching point: the scariest-looking number (BP 172/100) is NOT the most urgent problem here; the glucose of 3.6 is. 4. History Immediately available (notes, wristband, nurse handover) Only revealed if the trainee asks - Booked operation, diagnosis, medication list from pre-assessment - Pre-assessment fasting/medication instructions - Last GP BP readings: not included in the referral letter - "I took all my morning tablets as usual — I forgot about the instructions." (includes gliclazide, dapagliflozin, ramipril) - Last food: dinner at 21:00; water at 06:30 - Last HbA1c: "about a year ago" — none in last 3 months - No previous anaesthetic problems; no chest pain; walks 2 km - Symptoms now: sweaty, shaky, hungry 5. First abnormality — hypoglycaemia (glucose 3.6 mmol/L) What the trainee sees Sweaty, shaky patient; glucose meter reads 3.6. What it means Blood sugar below the safe floor of 4.0 mmol/L. Why it matters The brain depends on glucose; untreated hypoglycaemia progresses to confusion, seizures and coma. What could cause it Gliclazide taken while fasting; insulin; alcohol; sepsis. What to verify Repeat finger-prick (clean finger); check symptoms; ask what he took. If confirmed Initiate the hypoglycaemia protocol immediately (he is alert and can swallow, so the protocol's oral fast-acting carbohydrate may apply — in a fasting patient some protocols specify IV glucose; the nurse administers); recheck in 10–15 min. Note: taking glucose by mouth will itself affect fasting — the anaesthetist must know. Who to inform Nurse (now), anaesthetist (fasting and anaesthetic plan), senior surgeon. 6. Second abnormality — SGLT2 inhibitor taken today (euglycaemic DKA risk) What the trainee sees Medication history reveals dapagliflozin taken at 07:00. What it means An SGLT2 inhibitor plus fasting and surgical stress can cause ketoacidosis even when glucose is normal or low (euglycaemic DKA). Why it matters DKA is dangerous and can be missed because the glucose looks 'fine'. What could cause it Instructions not followed. What to verify Check capillary ketones; ask about nausea/abdominal pain; venous blood gas if ketones raised. If confirmed Ketones 0.9 mmol/L (raised, not DKA). The UK 2025 consensus advises omitting SGLT2 inhibitors the day before and the day of surgery, so surgery today is normally deferred; the anaesthetist/senior decide. Who to inform Anaesthetist and senior surgeon. Relationship to the earlier problem(s) Related: both are failures of the diabetes medication plan. Hypoglycaemia (A) plus SGLT2 (B) means starvation ketosis and drug-related ketosis add together — the ketone level must be watched while he is fasting. 7. Third abnormality — no recent HbA1c → result 76 mmol/mol What the trainee sees HbA1c sent (none in last 3 months, NICE NG45/CPOC); result 76 mmol/mol. What it means Average glucose over 2–3 months has been high (above the 69 mmol/mol / 8.5% optimisation threshold). Why it matters Poor control increases infection, wound and cardiovascular complications. What could cause it Undertreated diabetes, adherence. What to verify Confirm no interfering condition (anaemia, haemoglobinopathy). If confirmed Refer for optimisation before rebooking (CPOC). Who to inform Anaesthetist; GP/diabetes team via letter. Relationship to the earlier problem(s) B + C: poor control plus a multi-drug regimen that he could not follow safely → the peri-operative diabetes plan needs redesign, not just a new date. 8. Prioritisation — what is the most important problem right now? Priority Problem Why it is ranked here 1 — Immediate Hypoglycaemia 3.6 mmol/L Disability (D in ABCDE): can deteriorate within minutes to confusion/seizure; quick and simple to treat. 2 — Potentially serious SGLT2 taken today; ketones 0.9 Risk of euglycaemic DKA during fasting/surgery; needs monitoring, and today's surgery is unlikely to proceed (the anaesthetist decides). 3 — Optimisation HbA1c 76 mmol/mol Not dangerous today, but a recognised reason to optimise before planned surgery (CPOC). Priority Problem Why it is ranked here 4 — Important, non-urgent BP 172/100 Below the AAGBI/BHS 180/110 threshold: on its own would NOT stop surgery; needs GP follow-up. 9. Trainee decision process (chronological) Decision 1 What do I notice? Sweaty, shaky, glucose 3.6 What does it mean? Hypoglycaemia What do I check? Repeat reading; alertness; can he swallow? What do I do? (within my role) Ask nurse to start the hypoglycaemia protocol now (oral fast-acting glucose) Who do I tell? Nurse; then anaesthetist What happens next? Recheck at 10–15 min: 5.8 mmol/L, symptoms resolve What changes if confirmed? Fasting status changes (oral glucose) — anaesthetist must decide Decision 2 What do I notice? "I took all my tablets" What does it mean? Gliclazide and dapagliflozin taken What do I check? Exact drugs and times What do I do? (within my role) Check capillary ketones Who do I tell? Anaesthetist What happens next? Ketones 0.9 What changes if confirmed? Surgery today not appropriate per guidance Decision 3 What do I notice? BP 174/102 What does it mean? Raised, but below 180/110 What do I check? Repeat after rest; GP readings What do I do? (within my role) Document; not a reason by itself to cancel Who do I tell? Anaesthetist in the same call What happens next? Repeat 172/100 What changes if confirmed? None today; GP follow-up Decision 4 What do I notice? No HbA1c in 3 months What does it mean? Optimisation status unknown What do I check? Send HbA1c What do I do? (within my role) Await result Who do I tell? — What happens next? 76 mmol/mol What changes if confirmed? Optimise before rebooking Decision 5 What do I notice? Overall picture What does it mean? Medication plan failed + poor control What do I check? — What do I do?
